title: ‘Room to Spare,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
detail:
‘Room to Spare,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
TipRanks
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:52 PM EST 3 min read
ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

For most of this year, the big question around Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) was whether it could pay for its data center ambitions. The company now says it can. In a Nov. 20 statement, it said all the funding for its OpenAI contract is in place. That message, along with Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia, sent the stock sharply higher on Monday. The rally didn't last. A broad AI selloff on Tuesday and Wednesday wiped out the gains, and Oracle goes into the Thanksgiving break close to the 52-week low it hit midweek.

At about $104, the shares sit roughly 68% below their September 2025 record close.

Investor Louis Gerard still sees the balance sheet as the main problem. He just thinks it has become a smaller one. At its Oct. 28 Investor Day, Oracle promised to limit new capital raised through FY30 to $20 billion, half stock and half debt, and on Nov. 2 it raised the whole amount. Together with the $20 billion stock program it finished in the fiscal first quarter, that brings outside funding for fiscal 2027 to about $40 billion, which is what management said to expect back in June. For Gerard, a fixed limit is easier to live with than a funding need nobody can size.

The money came at a cost. Shareholders were diluted by 86 million new shares sold at $116. Oracle had also said in June that it didn't plan to raise more debt in 2026, and that turned out to be wrong. Borrowing got more expensive too. Notes due 2029 yielded about 4.6% when Oracle sold them in February, compared with roughly 7% this month. The ratings agencies still have Oracle at investment grade, but bond buyers are charging it rates closer to junk.

The cap only covers the stock and bond markets. Until free cash flow turns positive, which Oracle expects in the second half of FY28, vendor financing and customer prepayments have to fill the gap. Prepayments made the first quarter look better than it was. Of the record $23.1 billion in operating cash flow, $11.4 billion came from customers paying in advance. Without that, free cash flow would have been about negative $16.8 billion instead of negative $5.4 billion.

Meanwhile, Gerard's biggest worry is OpenAI. S&P estimates it accounts for about half of Oracle's backlog. OpenAI's latest round was also smaller and cheaper than it first wanted. CNBC reported $15 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, against an original goal of $30 billion at $1.4 trillion.

Gerard sees power as a second risk. Oracle delivered 850 megawatts in the fiscal first quarter, short of the nearly 1 gigawatt it had pointed to. Hitting its goal of about 10 gigawatts by the end of FY28 means delivering about a gigawatt a quarter.

Take a hypothetical 63-year-old retiree who watches AI stocks swing this fall. She moves $700,000 of her 401(k) out of equity funds and into her plan's investment-grade corporate bond fund. She thinks bonds are safe. If that fund drops 5%, she loses $35,000. She owns a market-priced asset, and nothing guarantees its value.

fizkes / Shutterstock.com
What Her "Safe" Fund Owns

An investment-grade corporate bond fund holds the debt of hundreds of large companies. A common stand-in for the category is the iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (NYSEARCA:LQD). Its latest portfolio filing lists bonds from major telecom and technology companies (holdings as of August 31, 2026). Several of those companies are among the biggest spenders on AI.

Two things move the price of those bonds every day. One is interest rates. The other is credit spreads, which are the extra yield investors want for lending to a company rather than to the U.S. Treasury. If either one goes up, bond prices go down, even when every company pays on time. This fall the 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.3% in early October. It has since come down to 4.9%.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) shares sank 5.13% to $103.88 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, after touching $99.34, a new 52-week low, as the cost of insuring its debt hit a record. Five-year credit default swaps reached 360 basis points, based on S&P Global Market Intelligence data, up from 35 basis points in mid-2025 and 154 at the end of 2025.

The operating numbers still look powerful on paper. Remaining performance obligations stand at $664 billion, and fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion as cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 120% to $7.4 billion. The friction is funding. Oracle said on November 20 that the financing outlined at its investor day, including vendor financing, is in place after a $20 billion raise split between equity and debt, with shares sold at $116. Wednesday's close sits more than 10% below that placement price and about 58% under the 52-week high of $250.25.

The swap market is now pricing Oracle more like a leveraged infrastructure developer than a software franchise, and that matters because every new data center needs capital long before it earns revenue. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 89/100, pairing elite profitability with a weak balance sheet that has deteriorated as borrowing grew. GF Value is $202.75, implying a 48.8% discount, but GuruFocus labels the shares a possible value trap, which fits a story where backlog is abundant and free cash flow is not. The next test is fiscal second-quarter results in December, where capex, free cash flow and any new financing will decide whether the swap spread keeps widening.

The swap move reflects a change in Alphabet's cash profile. Third-quarter capital spending reached $51.4 billion, and free cash flow came in at negative $9.1 billion. A consensus compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence does not see Alphabet generating free cash flow again until 2029. Hotter-than-expected October inflation data, with core PCE prices up 3.3% from a year earlier, added pressure on long-duration growth names the same morning.

For a company long valued on cash generation, three more years of expected negative free cash flow changes the math: the payoff from AI infrastructure now has to outrun the cost of financing it. Alphabet's balance sheet can carry that load, but credit markets are signaling less tolerance. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 98/100, reflecting elite profitability and a strong balance sheet. For a few minutes on Wednesday, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) changed hands at $99.34, its first trade under $100 since December 2023. It closed at $103.88, while the consensus analyst target of $236.18 implies about 127% upside.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images

Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% last quarter, and remaining performance obligations (Oracle's signed backlog) reached $664 billion. That growth is expensive, because Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter and posted free cash flow of negative $5.4 billion.

Banks that financed Oracle-linked data centers are now trying to sell some of those loans below face value. The stock's slide reflects how investors are now pricing the cost of the expansion.

Banks Are Selling Oracle-Linked Loans Below Face Value

HSBC (NYSE:HSBC) sold its roughly $300 million piece of the $18 billion Project Jupiter construction loan at about 85 cents on the dollar. Jupiter is an Oracle-linked New Mexico campus.

That sale followed a force majeure notice Oracle sent to the developer, a formal claim that events outside its control are disrupting the work. Oracle fell 4.99% the day the sale showed up.

ING (NYSE:ING) is auctioning off about $500 million of data-center loans that include Jupiter debt. Societe Generale is shopping about $300 million tied to Wisconsin and Texas projects, quoted above 90 cents.

title: How Will Oracle's Heavy AI Spending Shape the Stock's Cash Flow Trend?
detail:
How Will Oracle's Heavy AI Spending Shape the Stock's Cash Flow Trend?
Vasundhara Sawalka
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 8:41 AM EST 3 min read
ORCL
AMZN
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Oracle Corporation's ORCL AI infrastructure buildout is set to keep free cash flow under pressure through fiscal 2028, even as operating cash generation and contracted demand lay the groundwork for a reversal later.

In first-quarter fiscal 2027, operating cash flow hit a record $23 billion, up 184% year over year. However, capital expenditures surged to $28.5 billion from $8.5 billion, pushing free cash flow to negative $5.4 billion. Customer prepayments of $11.4 billion cushioned the outflow. The spending is translating into capacity, with Oracle delivering 850MW of additional data center capacity in the first quarter. Remaining performance obligations jumped $209 billion year over year to $664 billion, aided by more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts that carry no incremental impact on capital-raising plans.

Its guidance signals that the cash strain is far from over. Oracle expects fiscal 2027 capex of $90-$95 billion, with spending not linear through the year. Fiscal 2027 total revenues are projected to be at least $90 billion, with non-GAAP EPS of $8.10. Second-quarter total cloud revenues are expected to rise 65-71% in USD.

On its Oct. 28, 2026 Investor Day, Oracle flagged fiscal 2027-2028 as the peak capex period, with spending declining in fiscal 2029. Free cash flow is expected to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reach at least $30 billion in fiscal 2029, when growth becomes self-funded.

Oracle capped new capital-markets funding through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, split between $10 billion each in equity and gross debt, over and above the $20 billion equity raise completed in the first quarter. Vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and prepayments should ease upfront cash needs.

Still, data center delivery execution, shareholder dilution and elevated leverage, with net debt to adjusted EBITDA targeted below 3.5 times only by fiscal 2029, remain key watchpoints.

How ORCL's AI Spending Compares With MSFT and AMZN

Oracle is not alone in absorbing heavy AI spending. Microsoft MSFT generated $58 billion of operating cash flow in first-quarter fiscal 2027, exceeding Microsoft's additions to property and equipment, which rose to $39.4 billion from $19.4 billion. Amazon AMZN faces sharper pressure, with trailing 12-month free cash flow swinging to an outflow of $42.4 billion, even as operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. Amazon continues to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion. While Microsoft funds its buildout from internal cash generation, Oracle, like Amazon, is currently spending beyond operating cash flow, making disciplined execution critical.

Oracle (ORCL) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.

Shares of this software maker have returned -28.1% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -5.7% change. The Zacks Computer - Software industry, to which Oracle belongs, has lost 8.1% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

For the current quarter, Oracle is expected to post earnings of $1.88 per share, indicating a change of -16.8% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -0.1% over the last 30 days.

The consensus earnings estimate of $8.12 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +6.4%. This estimate has changed -0.1% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $10.95 indicates a change of +34.8% from what Oracle is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.7%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Oracle is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).
